Index form: Wi∣μi,σi∼Normal(μi,σi2)μi=β0+β1Tilog⁡(σi)=γ0+γ1Ti \begin{aligned} W_i \mid \mu_i,\, \sigma_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu_i,\, \sigma_i^2) \\ \mu_i = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} \, T_i \\ \log(\sigma_i) = \gamma_{0} + \gamma_{1} \, T_i \end{aligned} Matrix form: 𝐰∣𝛍,𝛔∼𝒩(𝛍,diag(𝛔2))𝛍=𝐗𝛃log⁡(𝛔)=𝐙𝛄 \begin{aligned} \mathbf{w} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu},\, \boldsymbol{\sigma} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\, \mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2)) \\ \boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} \\ \log(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) = \mathbf{Z} \boldsymbol{\gamma} \end{aligned} math, index form Wi∣μi,σi∼Normal(μi,σi2),W_i \mid \mu_i,\, \sigma_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu_i,\, \sigma_i^2),μi=β0+β1Ti,log⁡(σi)=γ0+γ1Ti,\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, T_i, \qquad \log(\sigma_i) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1\, T_i, matrix form 𝐰∣𝛍,𝛔∼𝒩(𝛍,diag(𝛔2)),\mathbf{w} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu},\, \boldsymbol{\sigma}   \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\, \mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2)),𝛍=𝐗𝛃,log⁡(𝛔)=𝐙𝛄.\boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{X}\,\boldsymbol{\beta}, \qquad   \log(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) = \mathbf{Z}\,\boldsymbol{\gamma}. piece R call produced one piece math. left half drm_formula() (body_mass ~ temperature) became mu line; right half (sigma ~ temperature) became log-sigma line; family = gaussian() choice became distribution line pinned identity link mu. what: Pitfall 1: The intercept is not “the average response”
title: Reading factors, dummies, and interactions
text: Symptom. reviewer asks intercept means; author answers “average body mass”. number way compared mean(dat$body_mass), now everyone confused. Diagnosis. body_mass ~ sex + body_size, intercept expected response reference level every factor zero every continuous predictor. fit sex = factor(female, male) means “expected body_mass FEMALE body_size = 0”. overall mean unless sexes balanced body_size already centred zero. Rule thumb. Read intercept expected response reference factor level zero every continuous predictor.
code: n_p1 <- 80 sex_p1 <- factor(sample(c("female", "male"), n_p1, replace = TRUE)) bs_p1  <- runif(n_p1, 50, 150) dat_p1 <- data.frame(   body_mass = rnorm(n_p1, 30 + 5 * (sex_p1 == "male") + 0.2 * bs_p1, 3),   sex       = sex_p1,   body_size = bs_p1 ) fit_p1 <- drmTMB(   drm_formula(body_mass ~ sex + body_size, sigma ~ 1),   family = gaussian(), data = dat_p1 ) sym_p1 <- symbolize(fit_p1, context = "intercept reading")  # WRONG: read the intercept as the grand mean. #   "the average body mass is 12.0 g" -- it is not. # RIGHT: read the intercept as the reference cell. #   symbol_table() flags the reference level so this is auditable. symbol_table(sym_p1)

title: Reading factors, dummies, and interactions
text: Symptom. fit (1 | site) six sites reports tight confidence bands fixed effects. bands look precise data justify, reviewer asks computed. what: Pitfall 5: Dropping the intercept doesn’t always do what you think
title: Reading factors, dummies, and interactions
text: Symptom. user wants every cell mean directly, types y ~ 0 + sex + site thinking give sex × site cell means, surprised coefficients still look like contrasts. Diagnosis. y ~ 0 + sex one factor give cell means directly (one coefficient per level). adding second predictor, e.g. y ~ 0 + sex + site, gives “sex cell means PLUS site contrasts reference site”. non-orthogonality two factors without intercept rarely reader wanted. group_means(sym, = c("sex", "site")) returns every cell mean correctly regardless formula written. Group means Rows marked * 95% confidence interval excludes zero (CI method: wald). Rule thumb. two factors, safest way get cell means group_means(sym, = c(...)), hand-built intercept-less formula.

what: Pitfall 6: poly(x, 2) and I(x^2) are not the same
title: Reading factors, dummies, and interactions
text: Symptom. paper reports “slope body_size 0.18 g/mm (poly(body_size, 2)1 coefficient)”. number happens match expected linear slope, looks fine — column first orthogonal polynomial body_size, raw linear term. Diagnosis. poly(x, 2) produces two ORTHOGONAL columns: combination xx x2x^2 scaled two columns uncorrelated. first column “slope xx”. contrast (x^2) puts literal x2x^2 column design matrix alongside separate linear xx term, now linear coefficient slope x=0x = 0. two parameterisations carry information coefficient interpretations differ. Use whichever fits story. Rule thumb. Use poly(x, 2) want orthogonal columns (uncorrelated polynomial terms); use (x^2) want literal quadratic interpretation.
